ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Failure of MCI to fill up vacant posts 
 326. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be p leased to state: 
(a) whether after learning that the Medical Council  of India (MCI) has failed to 
implement 
 directions to fill up the vacant posts, the Delhi High Court has directed Health 
Secretaries 
eight States and Vice-Chancellors of ten universiti es to explain the reason for delay in 
plementing the orders; 
(b) if so, what were the reasons put forward by the  States for not complying with the 
orders of the High Court to fill all the vacancies in the Medical Council; and 
(c) what are the steps now being considered to impl ement the orders of the High Court 
to 
fill up all the vacancies? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Medical Council of India (MCI) is co nstituted by the Central Government 
as per the provisions of Indian Medical Council Act , 1956, under various categories 
through election/nomination. A Civil Writ petition - Dr. Girish Tyagi versus Union of 
India & Others was filed in the High Court of Delhi  alleging non-filling of vacancies of 
members in MCI. During the course of the hearing of  the case, the Hon'ble Court 
monitored filling up of vacancies of members of MCI  and gave directions on 28th 
September, 2006, to the universities to send the na mes of elected representatives against 
vacancies of Members of MCI to the Central Governme nt within ten weeks. The Hon'ble 
Court also directed the concerned State Medical Cou ncils/States to complete the election 
of members from amongst the Registered Medical Grad uates within one month and send 
the name of elected members to the Central Governme nt. Subsequently, action taken 
report on filling up of vacancies was submitted bef ore the Court by the Central 
Government. On 19th January, 2007, the Hon'ble High  Court irected concerned 
authorities of 10 universities and 8 State Governme nts who had failed to comply with the 
High Court order dated 28.09.07, to be present in t he Court on the next date of hearing 
along with the records on the subject. 
The State Government submitted before the Hon'ble H igh Court that due to non-
vailability of up-to-date State Medical Registers, adequate fund, non-appointment of

Returning Officers, the election process could not be completed. Also the universities 
submitted before the Court that the election proces s could not be completed as 
Senate/Court were nonexistent and in some other uni versities where these bodies existed, 
they did not meet for quite some time and, therefor e, the elction of Members of MCI 
could not be held. 
As per the directions of the Court, 110 out of 130 vacancies of Members of MCI have 
been filled up. A Statement indicating the occupanc y position of members of MCI is 
enclosed as statement.

SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Sir, I would like to inf orm the hon. Minister 
that after the High Court directives the MCI has fi lled up many positions. But bulk of the 
time is going in recognising new colleges, post-gra duate degrees, etc. I would like to 
know from the hon. Minisiter whether the MCI has ta ken any action against the doctors 
who are proved to have been medically negligent or involved in medical crimes. The 
legal and consumer courts have taken action against  many doctors across the country. But 
the people seem to have lost faith in the MCI as a watch-dog of medical ethics. How 
many complaints have been filed against the doctors  with the MCI and the State Medical 
Councils over the past five years? Against how many  doctors has the MCI actually taken 
action? 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, the Medical Council of India is responsible for 
the  quality of medical education in this country and, b y virtue of this, it goes around 
inspecting the institutions and recommend to the Go vernment whether to recognise them 
or to renew their registration and so on. As far as  individual medical negligence of doctors 
is concerned, the respective State Medical Councils  are responsible for their conduct. If 
there is any complaint agaist any doctors per se, they could complain to the respective 
State Medical Councils. If the State Medical Counci ls fail in their duties, the National 
Council could take actions against doctors of deregistering or de-recognition or suspension 
of their registration and so on and so forth. 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Sir, I would like to kno w from the hon. 
Minister whether the news reports that the Governme nt is toying with the idea of creating 
a separate Department of Medical Education in the M inistry of Health and Family 
Welfare are true and, 

Oral Answers [7 DEC. 2007] to Questions   3 
if it is so, how it will be different from the char ter of MCI. Will it undermine the 
authority of the MCI? 
DR. ANBUMANIRAMADOSS: Sir, the Medical Council of I ndia is currently 
responsible for the undergraduate courses by an Act  of the Parliament and the 
Government of India is responsible for the post-gra duate courses. In some of the 
countries, they have one common post-graduate board . In India, we have two authorities 
to regulate the post-graduate medical education; on e is the Medical Council of India and 
the second is the National Board of Examination. Ov er the years, unfortunately, the 
Medical Council of India-regulated postgraduate edu cation has not been recognised in 
many countries internationally except in the neighb ouring countries. But as far as the 
National Board of Examination is concerned, there h as been wider acceptance 
internationally because of the standards of educati on and its quality, and it follows one 
single pattern of examination throughout the countr y. In fact, the United Kingdom, some 
of the Middle-East countries and some other Europea n countries were voluntarily 
requesting for reciprocal recognition of these cour ses. To harmonise both these, we have 
set up a Committee under Dr. Ranjit Roy Choudhary. He has made some 
recommendations. Certainly, we have not taken any d ecision yet. We will take a 
comprehensive view of all the stakeholders and then we will take a decision accordingly. 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Sir, I would like to know from  the hon. Minister whether 
nonavailability of eligible doctors is the reason f or not filling up the vacancies. If so, is 
there any proposal to set up new medical colleges in various States? 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, when we talk of doctor' s community, health 
human resources, actually, it includes not only doc tors, but nurses, paramedics, dentists, 
ASHAs, ANMs, the Indian System of Medicine, Ayurved a, Siddha, Unani, all those are 
also here. So far as availability of doctors is con cerned, for example, there are nearly 
7,00,000 allopathic and MBBS doctors in this countr y. Out of which, only 10 per cent 
serve in the rural areas. Out of 7,00,000,70,000 se rve in the rural areas. So, there are 
doctors, but most of them are concentrating in citi es, metros and towns. There is a 
problem in rural areas. Some of the hon. Members ha ve also raised an issue about some 
students protesting against one year compulsory rur al posting, as well. Sir, 72 per cent of 
the people live in rural areas. They have only 25 t o 30 per cent access to health care, in 
fact, in these 60 years of post-Independence. So, t o revive this entire concept of rural 
health care infrastructure, we have now put up the National Rural Health Mission for 
improving the infrastructure as well as manpower an d putting up specialist doctors and 
students in the rural areas.                                                                                 
Coming to medical colleges, perse, Sir, there are approximately 270 medical colleges i n 
this country. Out of which, 180 are only in six Sta tes, that is, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, 
Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra.  Rest of the 23 States have nearly 
100 medical colleges put together. There is a huge lacuna in the States of Uttar Pradesh. 
Bihar, etc. Bihar has only eight medical colleges f or a population of 110 million. Uttar 
Pradesh has 16 and Madhya Pradesh has 8 of them. In  the North East also, there has been 
a huge lacuna. For this, we are now going in for ch anging the regulation so that even a 
district headquarters hospital, a Government hospit al, could start medical colleges by 
having public-private partnership in these hard are as, in these National Rural Health 
Mission areas, including the North East. So, when w e change the regulations, I am sure 
there will be a lot of medical colleges set up with  the participation of local Governments. 
In the Eleventh Five Year Plan also we have a lot o f funds allocated for helping the State 
Governments to set up these institutions and colleges.

DR. BIMAL JALAN: Sir, I just want to put a suppleme ntary question on the issue 
raised by Shrimati Shobhana Bhartia on post-graduat e education. I would like to know 
whether there is a proposal to take over post-gradu ate education or  set up a separate 
Government machinery to regulate or supervise post- graduate education. We all accept 
that the postgraduate education in our coutry is no t up to the standard that all of us desire. 
However, it seems to me that the Government taking it over is not going to improve the 
matter. Of the top, say, 25 universities in the wor ld, which we would like to compare with 
our universities, does any one of these universitie s come under direct control of the 
Government of that country? Let us take the 25 best  post-graduate medical universities in 
the world. Are there any countries like Europe, the  USA, the UK, where they come under 
direct control of the Government? 
DR. ANBUMANIRAMADOSS: Sir, I have already answered the first part of the 
question of the hon. Member saying that there is a Committee under Dr. Ranjit Roy 
Choudhury. In fact, today the post-graduate educati on comes under the Government of 
India. The Government of India runs it. The Governm ent is responsible for it. So far as 
under-graduate education is concerned, it is the re sponsibility of the Medical Council of 
India. Today, the Government is responsible for the  post-graduate medical education. 
After the recommendations of the Ranjit Roy Choudhu ry Committee, it is not that the 
Government is going to takeover anything like that.  In fact, it is going to be a body or an 
authority. If at all we do that, it will be done after wider discussions with the stakeholders. 
We are taking a decision on that. 
In reply to second part of the supplementary, I wou ld say, the top institutions of the 
world, like, the Harvard University, Johns Hopkins University, Stanford University, are 
all in the private sector in their respective countries. Also, some of the institutions in India 
are doing well. But the best institutions in the fi eld of undergraduate and post-graduate 
education are, today, in the Government sector. And  we tend to regulate as well as 
increase the quality of these institutions. We are going in for a lot of curriculum changes, 
as such, both for the undergraduate and post-gradua te education because the curriculum 
that we are following today is a little outdated. H ence we are going in for a new 
curriculum change according to the modern concepts, modern technology development.

Declining growth rate of agriculture 
*327. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Min ister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the growth rate of agriculture is declining; 
(b) if so, the comparative details thereof during the l ast three years alongwith the 
reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken to improve the situation of agriculture in future? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a ) to (c) 
Astatement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Agriculture growth rate is subject to f luctuations due to influence of a 
number of factors like monsoon, weather, water and quality of land, among others. As per 
data compiled by the Central Statistical Organizati on (CSO), the growth rate of agriculture 
and allied sectors during the last three years in t he country as measured in terms of Gross 
Domestic Product (GDP) at constant 1999-2000 prices  has been zero per cent in 2004-05, 
six per cent in 2005-06 and 2.7 per cent in 2006-07 . However, the average growth rate of 
the sector during the last two years has been 4.35 per cent. 
(c) The National Development Council (NDC) in its 5 3 rd  meeting held on 29* May, 
2007 reaffirmed its commitment to achieve 4 per cen t annual growth in the agricultural 
sector during the Eleventh Plan (2007-12) and resol ved that agricultural development 
strategies must be reoriented to meet the needs of farmers and urged the Central and State 
Governments to evolves strategy to rejuvenate agric ulture. Towards improving the growth 
in the agriculture sector, recently, the Government has done the following: 
• Launched the National Food Security Mission with an outlay of Rs. 4,882 crore for 
the Eleventh Plan period. It aims to produce additi onal 10 million tonnes of rice, 8 
million tonnes of wheat and 2 million tonnes of pul ses by the end of the Eleventh 
Plan. 
•  Launched the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY ), with an outlay of Rs. 25,000 
crore which aims at achieving 4% annual growth in t he agriculture sector during the 
Eleventh Plan period, through incentivising the States to invest more in the sector. 
• Established National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA) to assist and support in 
planning for rainfed areas. 
• National Policy for Farmers, 2007 was brought out. 
• Provided additional financial resources for irrigation. 
• Imparted strategic focus on the national agriculture research effort. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, my supplement ary pertains to 
growth

rate in agriculture. Cultivable land in the country  is shrinking year after year due to 
several reasons like urbanisation, land use for som e other purposes, infrastructure,

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: In fact, there was  a request in the

SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, as already mentioned in the  reply, in the Eleventh Plan 
under the National Food Security Mission, certain a dditional crops have been planned. As

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, what is the p rogramme of the 
Government in respect of those 36 districts where s uicide rates are high? Are you going

Oral Answers [7 DEC.  2007] to Questions   7 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, for those 36 districts, the  hon. Prime Minister has 
already announced a package. A package of Rs. 17,00 0 crores has already been 
announced. The real problem in these areas is non-a vailability of water and that is why, 
one major decision has been taken, to complete each  and every project, be it major, 
medium or minor irrigation. Substantial amount of m oney has been provided to the State 
Governments to complete these projects in time. If the percentage of irrigation in these 
districts is improved, the situation would definite ly change. That work has been started 
practically in all the States. 
DR. M.S. SWAMINATHAN: Sir, the whole question of de clining or static growth rate 
in agriculture is a matter of serious concern and s everal new initiatives that the hon. 
Minister has mentioned in his reply can make a cont ribution. But, there are two 
significant interventions which are needed if we wa nt to stop the decline in the growth 
rate. First is the soil health care. Soil health is  deteriorating in almost all parts of the 
country because lack of balanced fertilisation and no macro nutrients; most of the soil-
testing laboratories are not functioning. I am awar e that Agriculture is a State subject. 
These laboratories are under the control of State G overnments. But nevertheless, it is a 
rather serious matter. Second is water harvesting and water management. 
Sir, what I would like to ask the hon. Minister is this. There have been many 
suggestions by the National Commission, farmers and  others regarding soil health care. 
But, are there steps being taken seriously to ensur e that balanced fertilisation is 
promoted? There has been a demand from organic farm ers that the kind of incentives 
which are given to chemical fertilisation must also  be extended to organic farming, such 
as biofertilisers and so on. I think, that is very important if you want to stop the decline. 
The Eleventh Plan document talks about technology f atigue, extension fatigue. We 
cannot allow these fatigues. I want to compliment t he hon. Minister for his recent 
programme. But I want to particularly ask him wheth er it is possible to ensure that we 
accelerate the progress on the issue of soil health cards to farmers. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, that is one of the most imp ortant issues. It is true that 
we have gone into details about the overall perform ance of the State Governments in the 
area of soil testing. There are some districts wher e soil testing laboratories have been set 
up by the State Governments, but that is not suffic ient. That is why another 230 or 240 
soil testing laboratories will be set up in the rem aining districts. A major programme will 
be undertaken through the State Governments to prepare a soil health card. 
Secondly, we have set up, practically, in each and every district, except 4 or 5 or 7 or 
8, in the entire country, Krishi Vigyan Kendras. No w, these KVKs will be equipped with 
soil testing labs also. The KVKs have also been aut horised to take up the programme of 
soil testing. The cards will be prepared and that w ill be provided to farmers where it will 
guide them as to what type of balanced fertiliser u se should be there. There is another 
decision which is in the process, that is, regardin g providing the balanced fertiliser. You 
see, what happened is this. Our observation is, in some of the States like Punjab, Haryana 
and a number of other States, the farmers are using  too much urea and some other 
fertiliser which is, in fact, affecting the soil. T hat is why there is a need for the balanced 
fertiliser. Now, whatever facilities and whatever s ubsidies which we are providing have 
to be changed. There is a Committee under my chairm anship, consisting of the Finance 
Minister, the Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission and the hon. Fertilisers Minister, 
and we are going to take a final view about what ty pe of incentives should be provided 
for the balanced fertiliser. I think, we will be ab le to complete our work within one 
month's time.

SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, there are a number of quest ions asked in one supplementary. 
Firstly, this Government has given a lot of weighta ge for irrigation. The Budgetary provision 
for irrigation, for instance, in the year 2004-05 w as near Rs. 5,000 crores. Last year, it was Rs. 
7,000 crores and this year it is Rs. 11,000 crores.  This money will be provided to the State 
Governments and the money will not be provided to t he State Governments as a general fund. 
But, those projects which are nearing completion ha ve to be expedited and they have to be 
completed; just to complete these projects this additional financial support is being provided by 
the Government of India. 
Sir, another question was asked here about producti on. In fact, in the last three years, if you 
carefully see the total production situation, in th e foodgrains, in the year 2004-05, the total 
production was 198.36 MT. Last year, it was 208 MT and this year, it is 216 MT. So, every 
year, there is an improvement. There is a similar s ituation in oilseeds. In this particular year, 
there is a record production of cotton, there is a record production of soybean, there is a record 
production of sugarcane, So, there is improvement. 
The real problem is the pressure on land. 56 per ce nt of the population, practically, depends 
on agriculture and 80-82 per cent farmers are havin g the land below one hectare. It is our 
expectation that the farmer who has got just 2.5 ac res of land has to look after a family of five 
persons. As the hon. Member has said, 60 per cent o f the agriculture is rainfed and it is not an 
assured water. With unassured water, rainfed agricu lture, and just 2.5 acres of land, it is not 
easy at all to shoulder the responsibility of looki ng after a family of five persons. That is why, 
there is too much pressure on the agricultural land . Unless and until a certain percentage of this 
pressure is shifted elsewhere and that unit becomes  viable, it will be really difficult for any 
farming family. These are the real issues which we are facing today.

DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Sir, it is an irony, Mr. Chairman, Sir, that we have 
an Agriculture Minister who is no less a messiah of  kisans, still, the average growth rate 
mentioned is misleading. It is not the average grow th rate which will count for the farmer, 
Mr. Chairman, Sir. For him, the growth rate will co unt for each rabi and kharif and each 
crop. If an average depth is taken of a river, peop le have drowned because of taking into 
account only the average depth and not the depth at  many points. So, let us not talk of 
average growth rate, let us talk of growth rate of that year when it was zero. It is surprising 
to know why they did not commit harakiri, suicide, in total, in that year when the growth 
rate was zero. If there is zero growth rate in any industry, can it survive? My question is: 
Sir, particularly, do kisans, the annadata, commit suicide out of pleasure? 16,000 suicides 
take place every year! Every day, 200 suicides are there! I have a poignant cutting which, I 
think, will touch the heart of the Agriculture Minister. My question is: Is it a fact that on 1st 
November, in that dreadful night, one Mansukhani Da kani, 45, his wife, father and mother, 
four people, quietly left their house in the night,  went to the Somnath temple, entered the 
sea and ended their life because, in Saurashtra, th ey consider death better than debt? That

Special programme to check the declining sex ratio 
*328. KUMARI NIRMALA DESHPANDE: Will the Minister o f HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) is there a steep decline in sex ratio in India; 
(b) if so, what are the special programme taken up by his Ministry to change this trend; 
(c) what are the main reasons for this crises; and 
(d) what is the role assigned to NGOs to set things right? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Sex Ratio (SR) (number of females pe r thousand males) has increased 
from 927 to 933 from 1991 to 2001. However, the Chi ld Sex Ratio (CSR) has declined 
from 945 to 927 during the same period. State-wise Sex Ratio and Child Sex Ratio is given 
in the Statement (See below). 
Some of the reasons for low levels of sex ratio are  son preference prevalent in the 
society, neglect of the girl child resulting in hig her mortality, female infanticide and female 
foeticide. 
Sex determination techniques have been in use in In dia since 1975 primarily for the 
determination of genetic abnormalities. However, th ese techniques are widely misused to 
determine the sex of the foetus and subsequent abortions if the foetus is found to be female. 
In order to check female foeticide, the Pre-natal D iagnostic Techniques (Regulation and 
Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, was brought into o peration from 1st January, 1996. The 
Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Pre vention of Misuse) Act, 1994, has 
since been amended to make it more comprehensive. T he amended Act and Rules came 
into

force with effect from 14.2.2003 and the PNDT Act h as been renamed as "Pre-
conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Pro hibition of Sex Selection) Act, 
1994". 
The technique of pre-conception sex selection has b een brought within the ambit of 
this Act so as to pre-empt the use of such technolo gies, which significantly contribute to 
the declining sex ratio. Use of ultrasound machines  has also been brought within the 
purview of this Act more explicity so as to curb th eir misuse for detection and disclosure 
of sex of the foetus lest it should lead to female foeticide. The Central Supervisory Board 
(CSB) constituted in terms of the Act under the Chi rmanship of Minister of Health and 
Family Welfare has been empowered for monitoring th e implementation of the Act. The 
National Inspection and Monitoring Committee has be en constituted at the Centre to 
undertake field Inspections frequently and report to the concerned State/UT Governments 
to take corrective measures wherever shortfall or v iolations of the Act have been noticed. 
The National Support and Monitoring Cell advises th e Centre in putting in place a 
mechanism, including legal framework, for effective implementation of the Act. 
State level Supervisory Boards on the lines of CSB have been introduced for 
monitoring and reviewing the implementation of the Act in States/UTs. The State/UT 
level Appropriate Authority have been made a multi member body for better 
implementation and monitoring of the Act in the Sta tes. More stringent punishments are 
prescribed under the Act so as to serve as a deterr ent for minimizing violations of the 
Act. Appropriate Authorities are empowered with the  powers of Civil Court for search, 
seizure and sealing the machines, equipments and re cords of the violators of law 
including sealing of premises and commissioning of witnesses. It has been made 
mandatory to maintain proper records in respect of the use of ultrasound machines and 
other equipments capable of detection of sex of foe tus and also in respect of tests and 
procedures that may lead to pre-conception selectio n of sex. The sale of ultrasound 
machines has been regulated through laying down the  condition of sale only to the bodies 
registered under the Act. 
It is, nevertheless, recognized that mere legislati on is not enough to deal with this 
problem that has roots in social behaviour and prej udices. Various activities have been 
undertaken to create awareness against the practice  of pre-natal determination of sex and 
female foeticide through Radio, Television and prin t media units. Workshops and 
seminars are also organized through Voluntary Organ izations at 
State/regional/district/block levels to create awareness against this social evil. Training of 
the judiciary and other legal professionals are und ertaken to sensitize them on the issues 
related to PNDT Act. 
An amount of Rs. 5.00 lakh each has been given to 1 26 Members of Parliament (Lok 
Sabha and Rajya Sabha) from States of Chandigarh, D elhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal 
Pradesh, Punjab and Rajasthan to create public awar eness on sex selection and declining 
sex ratio by organizing exhibitions, seminars, work shops, trainings/orientation 
programmes for PRIs, SGHs, public meetings, debates , essay competitions, nukkad 
nataks, stage shows etc. 
The Government, on continuing basis, is monitoring and taking action to strengthen 
the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniq ues Act (PC & PNDT Act) as well 
as creating awareness on the issue through various IEC mechanisms though the active 
participation of the State/UT Governments, NGOs and other institutions.

DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: The meeting of the Central S upervisory Board 
(CSB), the highest board to regulate and enforce th e PNDT, is on 12th instant. As special 
invitees, Members of Parliament could also be calle d there. In the CSB, there are 
members from the NGOs, civil societies and some spe cialists are also there. The Ministry 
of Health, Government of India, is also involved wi th the religious leaders. I have 
personally attended some of the religious sects. Raths have also been going around in the 
affected States. In Punjab, involvement of Jatthedars of the Takht Shri Damdama Sahib 
and Anandpur Sahib in preaching and advocating the cause had been sought. In fact, we 
have been funding some of these programmes. We have  also been holding meetings with 
the National Minorities Commission to discuss steps  to improve sex ratio, with special 
focus on Punjab. Then, workshop had also been organ ized at Chandigarh by the Planned 
and Voluntary Health Association of India. Sensitis ation of MLAs with the CH; 
celebration of the Lohri festival for the newly born girl child, annually, b y the Women 
and Child Department; launching of the Balari Raksh ak Yojana, a State-funded scheme 
for preference of girl child, are some of the steps  that have been taken in this regard. So, 
we are actively coordinating with these religious l eaders, as such. Then, the melas are 
also held to spread the message. We ask the big rel igious sects also to preach the 
improtance of girl child. 
PROR P.J. KURIEN: Sir, the most improtant reason fo r decline in sex ratio is female 
foeticide, which is prevalent mostly in the affluen t sections of the society. Spreading 
education and coordinating with the religious leade rs is good. But the strictest laws will 
act as a deterrent. And, the PNDT Act is already he re. The hon. Minister, in his r( )ly, 
says that this Act was implemented on 14.2.2003.  I  would like to know from the hon. 
Minister, after the implementation of this Act, how  many cases have been detected and 
how many prosecutions have been there? Sir, female foeticide is just terminating a life. It 
is nothing less than a murder. So, it should be tre ated as killing a born child. Will the hon. 
Minister consider to increase the quantum of punish ment, and also to make the 
punishment more stringent, where female foeticide w ill be treated as a murder of girl 
child, in order to deter the people from keeping away from such crimes? 

16    Oral Answers [RAJYA  SABHA] to Questions  
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, there are 403 ongoing c ases and 132 ultrasound 
machines have been seized and sealed. In this year,  about 125 cases have been reported, 
and there have been four convictions. The convictio n is low because it is a clandestine 
operation and the accomplices, both, doctor and the  patient, don't give away each other. 
That's why even under the PNDT and despite the CSB in existence, we have been 
empowering the State authorities to have decoy cust omers so that they could go and 
appraoch the doctors, frame them and book a case ag ainst them. But these are individual 
instances. We are sensitising the Judiciary. We hav e had workshops in Madhya Pradesh 
and in Delhi on Judiciary sensitisation because the  number of cases may be high but 
convictions are very few. Not only that, in the las t meeting of the CSB, a lot of 
recommendations were given by the hon. Members. Som e of them were even with regard 
to bringing amendments in the Act, which we are con tending to do. In this meeting, we 
are trying to finalise the desirable changes so tha t the penalty is more stringent. Hon. 
Members have been raising point about the implicati ons of that. Let me inform that there 
will not only be fine, but even life imprisonment t oo. So, all these recommendations, with 
regard to making the punishment more stringent, wil l be considered in the coming CSB 
meeting.

Oral Answers [7 DEC.   2007] to Questions    17 
Decision to corporatise the Delhi Milk Scheme 
*329. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Minister of A GRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has decided to corporatise the Delhi Milk Scheme; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a ) to (c) Yes, Sir. 
The Government has decided 'in principle' to corpor atise the Delhi Milk Scheme to 
provide more autonomy in its operations and managem ent, flexibility in financial matters 
having regard to the consumers and in the interest of organization for making it more 
efficient and viable. Expression of Interest (Eol) from reputed professional agencies to 
prepare feasibility report and Memorandum of Unders tanding (MoU)/Articles of 
Association (AoA) and other related jobs have been invited in the matter. 
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: What is the immediate reason  or rather provocation to 
corporatise the Delhi Milk Scheme? Have you found o ut any sort of financial 
irregularities or administrative lapses in it? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, this particular unit was lo sing for a number of years, 
and various Governments have taken certain decision s about it. In 1997-98, the Union 
Govemment had taken a decision to handover this uni t to the Delhi Government. But the 
Delhi Government was not ready to accept. Ultimatel y, the Delhi Government put certain 
conditions that they are ready to accept all liabil ities up to a particular date. They were 
insisting that the Government of India should take that responsibility. The Delhi 
Government was also insisting grant of adequate fun d for the modernisation of the plant 
and machinery. The Delhi Government has also insist ed redeployment of surplus staff of 
the DMS. So, these suggestions were not accepted by  the Government of India. And, 
ultimately, nobody was ready to take this unit. It is a unit, which is losing and the 
Government feels it requires improvement. Managemen t has to be improved and 
flexibility in the financial matters has to be give n. More autonomy should be given to this 
particular unit. There is no solution, but, ultimat ely, to accept, to corporatise this Delhi 
Milk Scheme That was the reason why this decision was taken. 
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Sir, my second supplementary  is this. Besides taking 
suggestions from reputed professional agencies, is the Government considering to look 
into some of the milk schemes in various States inc luding Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, 
Haryana and Punjab? I would also like to know wheth er the Government is considering 
going through the functioning of all these States. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: The Government is fully aware of  all these schemes 
because the Government has got very close rapport w ith the various milk schemes, which 
are, practicaly, run by most of the States. Here, t his particular Scheme was losing 
continuously. It is difficult for this Scheme to pr ocure milk because Delhi is not a 
producing centre. The Delhi unit has to depend on U ttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana and 
Punjab. All these States are developing their own s chemes; that is why, there are 
limitations to get milk for this particular unit. I f we corportaise it, then, probably, more 
efficiently, this unit will be managed; probably, t hey will be able to procure more, and 
they will be able to bring the losses down. That is  the reason why this decision has been 
taken. 

18    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
MR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, according to our information , the DMS seems to be doing 
very well in Delhi. It is-much more welcome to see that they are going to make it more 
autonomous. I am inclined to ask the hon. Minister how long it will take. Can you afford 
to give a time-frame before which the entire proces s will be over and it would be made 
autonomous? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Our efforts are to expedite this  process. As the hon. 
Member said this unit is doing very well, in fact, if we study the overall deficit for the last 
five years, you will find that it shows that is not  the position. In the year 2002-03, deficit 
for this unit was Rs. 8,65,00,000/-; in 2003-04, it  was Rs. 20 crores; in 2004-05, it was 
Rs. 39 crores; and, in 2006-07, it is Rs. 24 crores . So, the way this unit is losing money, 
there is no choice, but, ultimately, to improve the  overall working of the unit, and, that is 
why, the decision to corporatise this unit has been  taken. We will expedite it and see that 
as early as possible, it is implemented.

Breast feeding promotion measures 
*321. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be p leased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that breast feeding is crucial for the health and 
development of the infants and this holds immense benefits for the mothers as well; 
(b) whether lack of awareness on breast feeding among t he common people has been 
the major bottleneck in promoting this practice among the general public; and 
(c) if so, what is the action plan of Government to cre ate awareness among the general 
public about the immense benefits of breast feeding? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) The Government is aware that breast- feeding is important for the 
health and development of the infants and it has good benefits for the mothers as well. 
(b) The Government is also aware that improving awa reness among the common 
people on breast-feeding will promote breast feeding practices among the general public; 
* The National Guidelines on Infant and Young Child F eeding issued by Department 
of Women & Child Development form an integral part of  ICDS and the RCH 
programmes. These guidelines incorporate new norms of Infant Young Child 
Feeding i.e., exclusive breast feeding for the firs t six months (replacing the 4-6 
months age range of earlier guidelines), introducti on of complementary foods at six 
months continuing breastfeeding upto the age of two years or beyond. 
* The National Nutrition Policy adopted by the Govern ment of India under the aegis 
of the Department of Women and Child Development in  1993 laid due emphasis on 
nutrition and health education of mothers on infant  and young child feeding and 
effort to trigger appropriate behavioural changes a mong the mothers were 
considered as direct interventions for reducing malnutrition in children. 
* The Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of 
Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, pop ularly known as the IMS Act 
was enacted to protect, promote and support breast feeding. This Act has been 
further strengthened enhancing the protection level. 
Through this Act, the baby food manufacturers have been banned to promote sale of 
their infant milk substitute and infant food through print and media. The relevant 

Written Answers to [7  DEC.   2007] Starred Questions   23 
provisions of the Cable Television Networks (Regula tion) Amendment Act, 2000, 
also prohibits advertisements of infant milk substi tutes, feeding bottles or Infant 
foods through cable television service. India now h as one of the strongest 
legislations to protect breastfeeding from commercial influence. 
* The Tenth Five Year Plan, for the first time, inclu des goals for breast feeding and 
complementary feeding in the National Nutrition Goa ls. Emphasis on Infant 
feeding will continue during the Eleventh Five Year Plan. 
* The National Rural Health Mission and the Reproduct ive and Child Health II 
strongly support early initiation of breast feeding  and exclusive breast feeding till 
six months. 
* All trainings under the National Programme NRHM/RCH II have a strong 
component of training for breast feeding and comple mentary feeding. All medical 
officers, Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANM) and Aangan  Wadi Workers (AWW) in 
their trainings are taught the importance of breast feeding and are especially taught 
how to counsel and teach mothers on breast feeding and complementary feeding. 
(c) Keeping in view the need for awareness, the Dep artment of Family Welfare under   
its RCH II, is implementing the following interventions: 
* A nation-wide behaviour change effort to promote br eastfeeding by involving all 
grassroots workers viz. ASHAs, AWWs, ANMs, village practitioners, male 
workers, link volunteers etc., Panchayats, Self Hel p Groups (SHGs), agents of 
change. Opinion Leaders, Non Governmental Organisat ion's (NGOs), using all 
health related contacts to promote improved breastfeeding employing mass media. 
* Augment ANMs/AWWs contacts with mothers. Promote ho me visits by 
Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA)/AWWs in t he antenatal and postnatal 
period as a part of IMNCI activities and use contacts to promote breast feeding. 
* Use all ANM/male health worker contacts for feeding  counseling. Use 
immunization session, field visits of ANMs and male  health workers for feeding 
counseling. 
* Strengthen breast feeding promotion efforts at faci lities. Promote breast feeding at 
various healthcare facilities including Primary Hea lth Centres (PHCs), Community 
Health Centres (CHCs), First Referral Units (FRU) and district hospitals.  
* Improve feeding counseling skills of provider. Trai n ASHAs, AWWs, ANMs, 
Lady Health Visitors (LHVs), male workers, link vol unteers, as well as physicians 
(government, private, general) specialists, modern,  Indian Systems of Medicine) 
and nurses in lactation and feeding counseling tech niques through pre-service and 
in-service training and education. 
* Educating the providers on the IMS (Infant Milk Sub stitutes, feeding bottles and 
infant food, regulation, supply and distribution) Act. 
* Promote appropriate and adequate complementary feed ing. Strengthen the ASHAs/ 
AWWs role through supportive supervision and monito ring, use all health related 
contacts to counsel mothers about solid foods, emph asize portion size and calorie 
density, promote culturally acceptable, low cost, b alanced and locally available 
infant foods (prepare local lists for counseling). 
* Accelerated implementation of the child survival strategy, Integrated Management 
of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) besides other feeding interventions for 
all the children 0 month-5 years of age.

Health sector expansion and healthcare to old people 
*322. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that according to FICCI , India would require an 
investment of 78 billion dollars in the next decade  to fund the addition of approximately 
10,00,000 beds which are needed; 
(b) if so, with meager funding of 1 per cent of GDP on total healthcare system, how 
Government would achieve this target; 
(c) what healthcare system his Ministry is going to evo lve for the ageing people and 
senior citizens having chronic diseases; and 
(d) in what manner, Government is going to ensure that old age people get cheaper and 
accessible medical treatment? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) According to the Study Report  of Federation of Indian 
Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), India wo uld require an investment of US $ 
77.9 billion in the next decade to fund the additio n of approximately 10,00,000 beds by 
2012. The study further states that the Government and Private Players need to focus on 
their core competencies/responsibilities, work toge ther to reduce inefficiencies and 
complement each others efforts. 
Presently, the public spending on health, as a percentage of GDP is in the vicinity of 1 . 
The National Common Minimum Programme has mandated that the Government will 
raise public spending on health to atleast 2-3% of GDP over the next five years with focus 
on primary healthcare. The strategy being adopted i n the Eleventh Plan is likely to 
enhance the levels of public health spending as a p er cent of GDP. This strategy aims at 
promoting comprehensive primary healthcare under th e National Rural Health Mission, 
develop tertiary healthcare facilities under Pradha n Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana 
(PMSSY) and concrete measures to arrest HIV/AIDS an d other communicable and life 
style diseases. 
The National Policy for Older Persons (NPOP), 1999 mandated separate beds for the 
elderly at various levels of health Care delivery s ystem. At present, elderly are being 
provided health care facilities through/as part of general health care delivery system, 
which is almost free of cost. The Eleventh Five Yea r Plan envisages implementation of 
the National Programme for Health Care of the elder ly to address the health care needs of 
the elederly population. It is proposed to establis h two National Institutes of Ageing in the 
country under this programme. These Institutes woul d be responsible for providing state 
of the art health care facilities to the elderly in  a comprehensive manner. In addition, 
research and training in the field of Geriatrics/Ge rontology would also be undertaken in 
these Institutes. 
Comprehensive specialist/super specialist care in t he identified speciality would be 
provided at the State medical colleges and district  hospitals for the elderly. There is also a 
provision of mobile Medical care for the elderly in  the community who are bed ridden/ 
mmobile.

months in advance against the payment of a premium; 
(d) if so, the rationale for such provisions in the scheme; and 
(e) what steps are being taken to ensure that the seats  are made available to passengers 
traveling in emergency? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) an d (b) The Tatkal 
reservation system has been reviewed from time to t ime and the following modification 
has been made in this scheme recently:— 
With a view to improve Tatkal utilization in those trains in which the utilization of 
Tatkal accommodation is less than 50% in sleeper cl ass on an average for the whole 
financial year and to save the botheration of gener al wait listed passengers to go to 
reservation counter again to book berths under Tatk al scheme, instructions have been 
issued to Zonal Railways that wait listed passenger s of such trains should be given an 
opportunity to opt for booking under Tatkal Quota ( upto 50% of total Tatkal quota) at the 
time of buying their waitlist ticket itself. This s cheme has been introduced on an 
experimental basis for a period of six months.

only

passengers to go to reservation counter again to bo ok berths under Tatkal scheme and 
also to optimize the utilisation of Tatkal berths. 
(e) The scheme is not likely to affect the normal avail ability of Tatkal berths as the 
occupation level of Tatkal quota in trains covered under the scheme is below 50% and 
only 50% of Tatkal quota has been earmarked for waitlist passengers.

Incentives to farmers 
*332. SHRI VARINDER SINGH BAJWA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any specific incentives have been given to the farmers of wheat producing 
areas this year so as to ensure increased production of wheat in the country; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the likely expenditure incurred/to be incurred thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a ) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. A Centrally Sponsored National Food Security M ission—Wheat (NFSM-Wheat) has 
been launched for implementation from Rabi, 2007-08  in 138 identified districts of nine 
states namely Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan, 
Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal with an aim to increa se production of wheat by 8 million 
tones by the end of Eleventh Plan (2011-12) in the country. 
Under this Mission incentives are provided for demo nstrations of improved package of 
practices; seed replacement; micronutrients; gypsum ; zero till seed drills; rotavators; pilot 
project on community generators for irrigation in s hallow water table areas; diesel 
pumpsets; farmers trainings; award for best performing districts, new initiatives etc. 
During the current rabi season (2007-08) an amount of Rs. 163.393 crore has been 
approved, out of which an amount of Rs. 89.20 crore s has been released. Besides, 
5,10,480 number of wheat minikits of latest varieti es (5 kg each) with a cost of Rs. 5.10 
crore have also been allocated. 
In addition to this, Integrated Cereals Development  Programme—Wheat (ICDP-
Wheat) has been under implementation on 90:10 shari ng basis between GOI and 
implementing states in non-NFSM districts through M acro Management Mode of 
Agriculture. Under this Scheme incentives are provi ded for distribution of seeds, 
propagation of improved production technologies, in tegrated pests management, training 
of farmers, farm implements, sprinkler sets, etc. B esides, Frontline demonstrations are 
also organized by the ICAR on farmers' fields on 100 per cent GOI assistance.

(d) the details of cereals that are going to be worst affected due to climate change; and 
(e) what plans his Ministry has to overcome this situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) No, Sir. There is considerabl e uncertainty about the 
magnitude of loss, however, preliminary studies suggest that loss in cereal production due 
to climate change could be 5 to 40% by the end of 2100 AD. 
(b) ICAR is studying the possible impact of climate cha nge on cereal production 
through Network Project on "Impact, Adaptation and Vulnerability of Indian Agriculture 
to Climate Change" at different ICAR Institutes. 
(c) There is no direct analysis of production decline i n the last few years due to 
climatic change/variability. However, it is well kn own that increased temperature in 
February and March have caused some production decline in recent years. 
(d) Wheat is likely to be more affected due to climate change. 
(e) During Tenth plan period ICAR has initiated a Netwo rk Project on "Impact, 
Adaptation and Vulnerability of Indian Agriculture to Climate Change" at different ICAR 
Institutes/State Agricultural Universities. Emphasi s has also been given during XI plan 
period to strengthen the existing institutional net work to cope with the challenges posed 
by climate change. 
Need to import rice 
1945. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of AGR ICULTURE be pleased 
to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that production of rice would not be able to meet domestic 
needs and that the country may have to resort to import of rice; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether the production of wheat is sufficient to me et requirement of those rice 
eaters switching to wheat; 
(d) if not, the steps being taken to ensure self-sufficiency in rice and wheat; and 

Written Answers to [7 DEC. 2007] Unstarred Questions   41 
(e) whether the shortfall in rice production would result in rice eaters switching to 
wheat? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (e) On the basis of the mo nthly per capita quantities of 
consumption reported in the National Sample Survey 61 st Round Report on "Household 
Consumption of Various Goods and Services in India,  2004-05" and the population 
projections given by the Office of the Registrar Ge neral of India, the consumption 
requirement of rice in the country during 2006-07 i s estimated at 88.25 million tonnes 
which also include seed, feed and wastage. As again st this requirement, the production of 
rice during 2006-07 (4th advance estimates) is esti mated at 92.76 million tonnes, India is 
a net exporter of rice. 
Following the said approach, consumption requiremen t of wheat in the country during 
2006-07 is estimated at 67.60 million tonnes as com pared to its production of 69.35 
million tonnes during the crop year 2005-06 which i s available for consumption during 
marketing year 2006-07. The country imported 6.08 million tonnes of wheat during 2006-
07 to augment the buffer stock. However, during 200 6-07 the country produced 74.89 
million tonnes of wheat which will be available for  consumption during 2007-08 against 
estimated requirement of 68.59 million tonnes. 
To increase the production of rice and wheat, the I ntegrated Cereals Development 
Programmes (ICDP) in rice and wheat based cropping systems have been under 
implementation since October 2000 in the country. H owever, in order to increase the 
production of rice and wheat further, recently a Ce ntrally Sponsored Scheme "National 
Food Security Mission" (NFSM) has also been launche d from 2007-08 in the country. It 
aims at increasing the production of rice by 10 mil lion tonnes and wheat by 8 million 
tonnes by the end of the Eleventh Plan, i.e., by 2011-12 through area increase and 
productivity enhancement in targeted districts of the country.

pleased to state:

NFSM in Jharkhand 
1951. MS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of AGRIC ULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the number of districts of Jharkhand which are incl uded in National Food security 
Mission (NFSM) alongwith the details thereof, crop-wise; 
(b) how much productivity of foodgrain would be increas ed in Jharkhand due to the 
inclusion of the districts in NFSM; and 
(c) whether Government has a perspective plan to increa se the production of foodgrain 
by way of improved seeds, fertilizers , levelling o f land, etc. alongwith the details thereof, 
crop-wise and areawise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) Centrally Sponsored S cheme "National Food Security 
Mission (NFSM)" has been launched in 305 identified  districts of 16 States from Rabi 
2007-08 with an aim to increase the additional prod uction of 20 million tonnes of 
foodgrains, comprising of 10 million tonnes of rice , 8 million tonnes of wheat and 2 
million tonnes of pulses by the end of Eleventh Pla n (2011-12). The National Food 
Security Mission (NFSM) has three components viz. National Food security Mission-Rice 
(NFSM-Rice), National Food Security Mission-Wheat ( NFSM-Wheat) and National Food 
Security Mission-Pulses (NFSM-Pulses). 

Written Answers to [7 DEC. 2007] Unstarred Questions   63 
The major interventions under NFSM are demonstratio ns on improved production 
technologies; distribution of quality seeds of high  yielding varieties & hybrids; 
popularization of newly released varieties through seed minikits; support for micro-
nutrients, gypsum, zero tillage, rotavators, conowe eders and other farm implements; 
integrated pest management; integrated nutrient man agement; water lifting and moisture 
saving device; training and mass media campaign inc luding award for best performing 
districts etc. Besides, the pilot projects on commu nity generators, management of blue 
bulls and demonstrations of International Crop Rese arch Institute for Semi Arid Tropics 
(ICRISAT) technologies are also included. The ident ified districts are given flexibility to 
adopt the area specific technological interventions suited to their local conditions. 
In Jharkhand five districts namely Simdega, Singhbh usm (W), Ranchi, Gumla and 
Hazaribagh have been identified under NFSM-Rice. Wi th inclusion of above five 
districts, it is projected that, subject to favoura ble climatic condition and rainfall 
behaviour, the productivity level of rice in these districts will come at least at par with 
the State average productivity by the end of Eleventh Plan.

improvement of agricultural production and producti vity and enhancement of the income 
of the farmers are some of the major thrust areas i dentified by the Government for 
focused and concerted action. In order to achieve t hese objectives, the "National Policy 
for Farmers", incorporating the key recommendations  of the National Commission on 
Farmers, has been approved by the Government. In Ad dition, a number of 
programmes/schemes are already under implementation . Two new schemes, i.e. 
"Rashtriya Krishi Vikas yojana", which aims to achi eve 4% annual growth in the 
agriculture sector during the Eleventh Plan Period by ensuring a holistic development of 
agriculture and allied sectors with an objective, inter alia, to incentivise States to increase 
public investment in agriculture and allied sectors  and the "National Food Security 
Mission" to enhance the production of rice, wheat a nd pulses, with overall proposed 
allocations of Rs. 25,000 crore and Rs. 4882.48 cro re respectively have been launched 
recently, several other schemes, including "Nationa l Horticulture Mission" and the 
"National Rainfed Area Authority" have also been la unched by the Government, A 
comprehensive credit policy has also been announced  by the Government of India in

Irrigation management under Food Security Mission 
1966. SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased  to state: 
(a) whether Government has proposed to launch Food Secu rity Mission during the 
current year; 
(b) if so, the financial allocation for this purpose an d whether such mission would 
give prime importance for irrigation management, si nce lack of irrigation management is 
the main cause for the decline of food production; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. A Centrally  Sponsored Scheme "National 
Food Security Mission (NFSM)" has been launched in 305 identified districts of 16 
States from Rabi 2007-08 with an aim to increase th e additional production of 20 million 
tonnes of foodgrains, comprising of 10 million tonn es of rice, 8 million tonnes of wheat 
and 2 million tonnes of pulses, by the end of Eleventh Plan (2011-12). The National Food 
Security Mission (NFSM) has three components viz. National Food Security Mission-
Rice (NFSM-Rice), National Food Secrurity Mission-w heat (FSM-Wheat) and National 
Food Security Mission-Pulses (NFSM-Pulses). A Budge t allocation of Rs. 402.00 crore 
has been made during the year 2007-08 for the purpo se. Keeping in view the importance 
of irrigation in accelerating the production of whe at and pulses, provision for pilot 
project on community generators for irrigation in s hallow water table areas, diesel pump 
sets under NFSM-Wheat and distribution of sprinkler  sets under NFSM-Pulses has been 
made.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI

(c) The Ministry of Agriculture is implementing Centrally Sponsored Schemes namely 

78    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Ho rticulture in North Eastern and 
Himalayan States (TMNE) and National Horticulture M ission (NHM), aim to increasing 
the production and productivity of horticltural cro ps including Floriculture. Under these 
schemes, assistance is provided to the farmers for area expansion, production of quality 
planting material of elite cultivars, adoption of n ew technologies, integrated pest 
management, integrated nutrient management, etc. Be sides, National Horticulture Board 
is also implementing schemes which provide assistan ce for production of horticulture 
crops including floriculture. These measures are ex pected to enhance the production of 
floriculture crops in the country. In addition to t hese, the Government has taken the 
following steps for promotion of floriculture in the country:— 
(i) Agri-Export Zones: To promote the floriculture industry in key producing region, 
six agri-export zones (AEZs) have been set up, name ly, Tamil Nadu (two 
floriculture AEZs) and one each in Karnataka, Mahar ashtra, Sikkim and 
Uttaranchal. 
(ii) Post Harvest Infrastructure: APEDA sponsored c old storages have been set-up at 
various airports like Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Che nnai, Bangalore and 
Trivandrum, to help exporters store their produce s ince there usually is a time lag 
between the time the flowers arrive at the airport and are loaded onto the aircrafts. 
(iii) Expansion of Product Basket: Initiatives are being taken to diversify the product 
range from purely roses exports to gerberas from Ut taranchal, Carnations from 
Himachal Pradesh, Heieconias from Kerela, Tuberose and Marigold from West 
Bengal, etc. In addition, the export of exotic flow ers like anthuriums from the 
North-East (Mizoram, Meghalaya) have already commen ced. Also, a bulb 
multiplication project is underway in Uttaranchal f unded by the Government's 
ASIDE Scheme. 
(iv) Freight Subsidy: Since the high freight costs make the Indian floriculture exports 
uncompetitive, APEDA provides a Transport Assistanc e Subsidy to the exporters 
to offset the freight costs. This has proved to hel p the exporters in a big way and 
has substantially reduced their transaction costs and the airfreight cost disadvantage 
that they face vis-a-vis international competitors. A proposal has been subm itted to 
continue this scheme during the Eleventh Plan Period. 
(v) Market Facilitation Centre: APEDA had setup its  first MFC in the Netherlands in 
2001. This has been a key initiative to increase In dian fresh-cut flower exports. Due 
to the MFC's presence at the location where the max imum international trade takes 
place has provided Indian growers with a perspectiv e of changing trends, 
requirements of the market, etc. Further, the estab lishment of this Center has 
resulted in reduced rejection, improved quality and  presentation of our exports. In 
view of its success and experience gained, Governme nt now plans to setup such 
centers at Tokyo and Dubai to capitalize on the huge market opportunity. 
(vi) Modern Flower Auction Centre: To develop a mar ket locally (and a supply base for 
exports), APEDA has taken an initiative of setting up auction centers in Bangalore, 
Mumbai, Kolkata and Noida. The consolidation of sup plies would enable the 
importers in the international markets to source th eir supplies from these auction 
centers. The price transparency and prompt payments  would enable faster growth 
of the industry that would help build up the volume  necessary for competitive 
supplies to the international market.

state:

water to enable them to have second crops and meet the shortage of the grain in the 
country;

implementing an "Accelerated Irrigaiton Benefits Pr ogramme" (AIBP) since 1999-2000 
for motivating farmers for utilizing water resource s through minor irrigation schemes 
including lift irrigaiton from river/nala for speci al category States of North-Eastern 
regions, other hilly States namely Himachal Pradesh , Sikkim, Jammu & Kashmir, 
Uttarakhand and KBK districts of Orissa which are p redominantly inhabited by tribals. 
This scheme was extended from December, 2005 to non -special category States to 
include Minor irrigaiton scheme which serve tribal and drought prone areas. This scheme 
helps to grow the second crops through creating irr igaiton facilities in these areas to 
enhance the production of different crops. 
Surface minor irrigaiton (MI) schemes of States of North-East, Hilly States (Himachal 
Pradesh, Sikkim, Jammu and Kashmir and Uttaranchal)  and drought prone KBK districts

(iii) the development cost of these schemes per hectare is less than Rs. 1.00 lakh.

more than 50 hectare, which serve tribal areas and drough prone areas, are to be included 
under AIBP.

Allocation of foodgrains to BPL households in Kerala 
1983. PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Will the Minister of CONSU MER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of BPL households identified by the Government of Kerala; 
(b) the number of BPL households for which foodgrains at BPL rate are allocated; 
(c) the reasons for the difference, if any; 
(d) whether the Government of Kerala has represented to  allocate foodgrains at BPL 
rate to all identified families; and 
(e) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER A FFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD S INGH): (a) to (e) 
The State Govemment of Kerala reported in April, 20 07 number of BPL families in the 
State as 20.22 lakh. In November, 2007, the number of BPL families including AAY 
families has been reported as 20.85 lakhs. 
The Government of India allocates foodgrains to the  States including Kerala, for BPL 
families (including Antyodaya Anna Yojana Families) , worked out on the basis of 
poverty Estimates of the Planning Commission for 19 93-94 and Population Project of 
Registrar General of India for 1 st March, 2000 or the number of cards issued, 
whichever is less. 
The number of BPL families in Kerala on this basis is 15.54 lakh. Therefore, 
allocations of foodgrains to the State of Kerala un der the Targeted Public Distribution 
System (TPDS) are being made for 15.54 lakh BPL families. 
The difference in the number of BPL families used b y the Govemment of India for 
making allocations and those reported by the State Government is because the State 
Government has issued ration cards to higher number  of BPL families based on its own 
identification. 
The State Government has requested for increasing a llocations of foodgrains on the 
basis of BPL ration cards issued by it. Since the G overnment of india makes allocations 
of foodgrains to all the States and UTs based on th e above mentioned norms (1993-94 
poverty estimate and March, 2000 population estimat e), the request of the State 
Government has not been accepted.

(c) Efforts made by Government to increase the production of pulses 
(i)  Integrated Scheme of Oilseeds, Pulses, Oil Palm and Maize 
The Centrally Sponsored Integrated Scheme of Oilsee ds, Pulses, Oilpalm and 
Maize (ISOPOM) is being implemented from 01.04.2004 , in order to promote crop 
diversification, to provide focused approach and to  provide flexibility to the States 
in implementation, based on regionally differentiat ed approach. Implementation of 
production programme has helped in increasing the p roduction of pulses in the 
country from 128.60 lakh in 1989-90 to 142.3 (4th Advance Estimate) tonnes 
in2006-07. 
(ii) National Food Security Mission-Pulses 
In pursuance of the resolution adopted in the 53rd meeting of National 
Development Council (NDC), Government has recently launched National Food 
Security Mission (NFSM) comprising rice, wheat and pulses during XI Plan. In 
order to achieve additional 20 lakh tonnes of pulse s production, an area expansion 
of 2.47 million ha through intercropping with pigeo n pea, cereals, cotton, 
sugarcane, oilseeds, replacement of rainfed upland paddy during kharif and another 
2.0 million ha by utilizing rice fallows in major r ice growing states (in rabi) has 
been targeted during XI Five Year Plan under NFSM-P ulses. The NFSM-Pulses is 
being implemented in 168 district of 14 major pulses growing states. 
The major interventions of NFSM-Pulses are as under:— 
* Increasing seed replacement rate to 25% from pres ent level of 7-8% through targeted 
seed production programme of improved varieties/hybrids of pulses.

* Popularisation of improved production technologies through supply of critical 
inputs to the beneficiary farmers. 
* Demonstration of Integrated Nutrient Managment (INM ) and Integrated Pest

* Promotion of micro nutrients, gypsum application and bio-fertilisers. 
* Promotion of sprinkler irrigation to provide life saving irrigation of pulses. 
* Pilot project on tackling the menace of blue bull ( Neel Gai) which has emerged as a

* Extension, training and mass media campaign including awards for best performing 
districts/states. 
* Pilot project to enhance pulse productivity/produ ction through demonstration of

Sex ratio after implementation of PNDT Act 
2010. PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Will the Minister of HEALT H AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the child sex ratio and the comparat ive figures in 1991 census and 
2001 census, State-wise; 
(b) whether there is any change after PC and PNDT Acts have been implemented; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government proposes to bring in more string ent punishment, so that 
female foeticide is brought to nil; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and 
(f) if not, reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) A Statement is enclosed. (See below) 
(b) to (f) In order to check female foeticide, the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, wa s brought into operation from 1st 
January, 1996. The Act was amended as "Pre-concepti on and Pre-Natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 " and was published in the Official 
Gazette on 20.1.2003. 
2. The technique of pre-conception sex selection has b een brought within the ambit of 
this Act, since misuse of such technologies signifi cantly contributes to the declining sex 
ratio. Use of ultrasound machines has also been bro ught within the purview of this Act 
more explicitly so as to curb their misuse for detection and disclosure of sex of the foetus, 
so that it does not lead to female foeticide. 
3. The Central Supervisory Board (CSB) constituted as per the Act under the 
Chairmanship of Minister for Health and Family Welf are has been further empowered 
for monitoring the implementation of the Act. State  level Supervisory Boards on the line 
of the CSB has been introduced for monitoring and r eviewing the implementation of the 
Act in States/UTs. The State/UT level Appropriate A uthorities have been made a multi 
member body for better implementation and monitorin g of the Act in the States. More 
stringent punishments are prescribed under the Act so as to serve as a deterrent for 
minimizing violations of the Act. Appropriate Autho rities are empowered with the 
powers of Civil Court for search, seizure and seali ng the machines, equipments and 
records of the violators of law including sealing o f premises and commissioning of 
witness. The sale of ultrasound machines has been r egulated through laying down the 
condition of sale only to the bodies registered under the Act. 
4. Act prescribed Punishement for violations of its provisions as under: 
 
* Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 10,000. 
* For any subsequent offences, he/she may be imprison ed up to 5 years and fined 
up to Rs. 50,000/-. The name of the registered medi cal practitioner is reported by 
the Appropriate Authority to the State Medical Coun cil concerned for taking 
necessary action including suspension of the registration if the charges are framed 
by the court and till the case is disposed off. 
5. The Central Government is taking a number of mea sures to implement the Act 
through 
the active involvement of the State/UT Governments people's representatives, NGOs and 
other social organizations/institutions, by way of conducting sensitization and training 

124    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
programmes for the implementing agencies, including the judiciary, and organizing 
awareness programme through various IEC mechanisms. 
6. The positive impact of the above earnest endeavo urs of the Government in 
containing female foeticide and ushering healthy se x ratio would be known only after the 
next Census is carried out and made public.

2035. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has carried out any survey on th e prevailing health facilities 
and availability of infrastructure to the rural people of the country; 
(b) if so, the details of the parameters fixed for such survey and the outcome thereof; 
and 
(c) the initiatives taken by Government to improve the primary healthcare system and 
medicial facilities for the people living in the ru ral areas of the country particularly in 
Punjab and Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government of India undertakes periodic 
nationwide surveys for assessing the impact of the healthcare interventions and 
programmes. In addition, a Facility Survey in the c ountry has been conducted by the 
Government in two phases (1998-99 and 2003-04), whi ch assessed the existing situation 
of the healthcare facilities available in the Gover nment healthcare establishments at 
different levels in India in terms of infrastructur e, staff, supply and equipment in respect 
of 591 districts. 
The Survey covered various facility parameters at t he District Hospital, FRUs, 
Community Health Centres, Primary Health Centres and Sub-centres e.g.: 
* Status of the infrastructure (building, staff quarters, supply of water and electricity, 
toilet and phone facilities, vehicle availability etc.)

Primary Health Care System and provide medical faci lities to citizens in rural areas. The 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) is the main vehicle for these reforms. NRHM is a 
flag ship programme of the Government. It is being operationalized throughout the 
country, with special focus on 18 States which incl udes 8 Empowered Action Group 
States (Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisg arh, Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, 
Orissa and Rajasthan), 8 North-East States, Himacha l Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir. 
The main aim of NRHM is to provide accessible, affo rdable, accountable, effective and 
reliable primary health care facilities, especially, to the poor and vulnerable sections of the 
population. NRHM seeks to strengthen the Public Health delivery system at all levels. 
The Sub-centre and PHCs are proposed to be revitali zed through better human 
resource management, clear quality standards, bette r community support and an untied 
fund to enable local planning and action. The India n Public Health Standards define 
structural, personnel, equipment and management sta ndards and have been finalised for 
District Hospitals, CHCs, PHCs and SCs. 
All the facilities are also being provided untied f unds to enable the local management

representation. These societies are also being give n funding support under the NRHM to 
allow local action. 
As in the case of other States, the States of Punja b and Maharashtra have also 
operationalised the NRHM and funds have been releas ed to these States after appraisal of 
the Programme Implementation Plans (PIP) submitted by them.

2037. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the. Mi nister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is formulating any scheme to save girl child in the country; 
(b) if so, the details worked out, so far; 
(c) whether Government is reaching out to the rural population; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the present status i n rural areas in Andhra Pradesh, 
district-wise; and 
(e) what is the role of Panchayats in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMA-DOSS): (a) to (e) In order to check female foe ticide, the 'Pre-natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Ac t, 1994' was enacted w.e.f. 
1.1.1996. The Act and 

Written Answers to [7 DEC. 2007] Unstarred Questions    149 
the Rules framed thereunder were amended to address  the difficulties encountered in the 
implementation of the Act and to counter the misuse  of the techniques developed to 
select the sex of the child before conception. Whil e the amended Act was published in 
the Official Gazette on 20.1.2003, the amended Rule s came into effect from 14.2.2003. 
The objective of these amendments is to ban the use  of sex-selection techniques before or 
after conception as well as misuse of pre-natal dia gnostic techniques for sex selective 
abortions and to regulate such techniques. 
The State/UT level Supervisory Boards on the line o f the Central Supervisory Board 
at the Centre have been introduced for monitoring a nd reviewing the implementation of 
the Act in States/UTs. The State/UT level Appropria te Authorities have been made a 
multimember body for better implementation and moni toring of the Act in the States. 
Provision has been made for creation of similar App ropriate Authorities at the District 
Level for implementation of the Act. More stringent  punishments are prescribed under 
the Act so as to serve as a deterrent for minimizin g violations of the Act. Appropriate 
Authorities are empowered with the powers of Civil Court for search, seizure and sealing 
the machines, equipments and records of the violato rs of law including sealing of 
premises and commissioning of witnesses. The sale o f ultrasound machines has been 
regulated through laying down the condition of sale  only to the bodies registered under 
the Act. 
Incidentally, the Union Ministry of Women & Child D evelopment have informed that 
they have included in the Annual Plan for 2007-2008  a scheme for the survival and 
development of the girl child, viz. 'Conditional Cash Transfer for girl child with

2039. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister o f HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the maternal mortality rate and infant mortality rate in the country, State-wise; 
(b) the ranking of India on World MMR/IMR scale; 
(c) the number of kids and mothers dying every year/day; 
(d) the present infant mortality rate at birth, within one year and within five years of 
age, as a whole, State-wise and whether it has improved over last three years; and 
(e) what is the action plan of Centre to address this alarming scenario of MMR/IMR? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR ANBUM ANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) As per the latest survey report of R egistrar General of India (RGI-
SRS 2001-03) published in the year 2006, the Matern al Mortality Ratio (MMR) for India 
is 301 per 100,000 live births. As per the latest S RS estimates (2006), the IMR for India 
is 57 per 1000 live births. MMR and IMR for India a nd State-wise is at Statement-I and 
II respectively (See below). 
(b) As per the "Estimates of Maternal Mortality dev eloped by WHO, UNICEF, 
UNFPA 
and World bank, in the publication, 'Maternal Morta lity in 2005' ", 45 countries have an 
MMR higher than that of India. A list of these coun tries alongwith their MMR is at 
Statement- 
Ill. (See below). 
As per the UNICEF publication "State of the World's  Children, 2007" 54 countries 
have an IMR higher than that of India. A list of co untries with ranking as per their IMR 
is at Statement-IV. 
(c) MMR of 301 per 1,00,000 live births (RGI-SRS, 2 003) translates into 77,000 
maternal 
deaths per year or about 200 maternal deaths per da y. Estimated number of deaths of 
children (0-4 years) (2005) per year is about 2 million and deaths per day is about 5,500. 
(d) The present IMR is 57 per 1,000 live births (SR S, 2006); the Child Mortality rate 
(0-4 years) is 17.3 per 1,000 population of the cor responding age group (SRS, 2005). 
State-wise IMR and Child Mortality Rate (0-4 years)  are at Statement-II and V 
respectively. The IMR has shown an improvement over  the years 2004 to 2006. The 
Child Mortality Rate (0-4 years) has remained almos t the same between the years 2003 
to 2005. 
(e) The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) launch ed  by the Government of 
India  in the year 2005, in order to improve the av ailability of and access to quality health 
care including services for Child Health, Immunizat ion and Safe Motherhood, seeks to 
provide effective health care to rural population t hroughout the country with special 
focus on 18 ' States with weak public health indicators and/or weak infrastructure.  
In order to bring about a reduction in MMR and IMR,  the Government of India is 
implementing following key interventions all over the country: 
1. Under Maternal Health: Janani Suraksha Yojana (J SY), a cash benefit scheme to 
promote Institutional Delivery with a special focus  on Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
and SC/ST pregnant women; Appointment of an Accredi ted Social Health 
Activist (ASHA) for every village to facilitate in accessing of health care services 
by the community including pregnant women; operatio nalizing Community
